sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is a true vascular emergency of the eye, analogous to a cerebral stroke. It occurs when the main artery supplying the inner retina is obstructed, leading to acute ischemia. The foveola remains red (the 'Cherry-Red Spot') because it is thin and receives oxygen from the underlying choriocapillaris, while the surrounding infarcted retinal nerve fiber layer becomes opaque and white.

branches: Calcific: Heart valves, white/dull, more obstructive

sections.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
content: Intracellular edema of the inner 2/3 of the retina (Ganglion Cell Layer).
Pyknosis of nuclei and eventual necrosis of retinal elements.
Survival window: In primates, irreversible damage occurs after 90–240 minutes of total occlusion.
Cilioretinal artery presence (15–30% of population) may preserve the foveal region.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD): Rapidly present, often profound.
Cherry-Red Spot: Macular center remains red against white retina.
Box-carring: Segmentation of the blood column in retinal veins.
Cattle-tracking: Interrupted flow in retinal arterioles.
Narrowed Arterioles: Severe attenuation and straightening.
Optic Disc Edema: More common in the Arteritic (GCA) variety.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Strategy
content: 1. Immediate Clinical Exam & VA testing.
2. STAT ESR, CRP, and Platelets (Rule out GCA).
3. Multi-modal Imaging: OCT and FFA.
4. Systemic Workup: Carotid Doppler, Echocardiography (TEE preferred).
5. Neurology Referral: Evaluation for acute stroke (MRI/MRA).

rows: Marked delay in arm-to-retina & filling time

sections.title: Emergency Management Protocol
content: 1. Digital Ocular Massage: Firm pressure for 10-15s, then release (dislodge embolus).
2. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: 0.1-0.2ml removal using 30G needle at limbus.
3. IOP Reduction: Acetazolamide 500mg IV/PO + topical Beta-blockers/Alpha-agonists.
4. Vasodilation: Breathe into a paper bag (increase CO2) or Carbogen therapy.
5. Systemic: Aspirin 325mg and urgent Stroke Center transfer.

branches: Commotio Retinae: History of trauma (Berlin's edema)
BRAO: Focal whitening in a vascular distribution
Tay-Sachs / Storage Diseases: Bilateral, chronic, pediatric
Quinine Toxicity: Rapid onset, history of ingestion

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS: GCA Warning
content: Scalp tenderness or Jaw Claudication
New-onset headache in elderly patients
Proximal muscle aches (Polymyalgia Rheumatica)
Bilateral vision loss (indicates imminent disaster)
Elevated ESR (>50) or CRP (>10)

content.explanation: C: Cilioretinal sparing (sometimes), H: Hollenhorst plaques, E: Emergency workup needed, R: Red spot (macula), R: Reduced VA (acute/painless), Y: Yield (High stroke risk).

sections.title: Complications & Long-term Monitoring
content: Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI): Occurs in ~18% of cases (Rubeosis Iridis).
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG): Onset typically 4-12 weeks (the '100-day' window).
Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD): Less common than in CRVO.
Retinal Atrophy: Chronic inner retinal thinning on OCT.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The EAGLE Study investigated Intra-arterial Fibrinolysis (tPA). It found no significant visual benefit compared to conservative management and noted a higher risk of adverse events. Current consensus favors rapid stroke center evaluation. Newer studies are exploring Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) within 8 hours as a potentially effective adjunct.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: CRAO is an Ocular Stroke until proven otherwise—check the carotids and the heart.
In a patient under 50, consider thrombophilia workup, trauma, or vasospastic triggers (Migraine/Cocaine).
Digital massage should be done with a Goldman lens or finger to fluctuate IOP and 'flush' the clot.
If the cherry-red spot is missing but VA is NLP, suspect Ophthalmic Artery Occlusion (no choroidal flow).

sections.content: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is a true ocular emergency characterized by sudden, painless monocular vision loss. It represents the ocular equivalent of a cerebral stroke and requires immediate neuro-ophthalmic triage.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: CRAO is an infarction of the inner retinal layers due to blockage of the central retinal artery. The central retinal artery is an end-artery, meaning there is no collateral circulation. Retinal viability is lost after approximately 90-100 minutes of total occlusion.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Fundoscopy
content: Sudden, profound painless loss of vision (typically 'counting fingers' or 'hand motion').
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) — often profound.
Fundoscopy: 'Cherry-red spot' at the fovea (due to choroidal blood supply).
Retinal whitening: Edematous, necrotic inner retina.
Cattle-trucking (segmentation of blood flow in arterioles).

rows: Scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ESR/CRP elevation

sections.title: Emergency Protocols
content: Rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with STAT ESR, CRP, and Platelet count.
Immediate stroke workup (Carotid Doppler, EKG, Echo, MRI Brain) is mandatory.
Irreversible retinal damage occurs after 90-100 minutes of occlusion.
Rule out hypercoagulable states in patients under 50 years of age.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Ocular massage (digital pressure to induce movement of embolus).
Step 2: Lower Intraocular Pressure (Topical timolol, acetazolamide 500mg IV).
Step 3: Paracentesis (if within 2-4 hours, though efficacy is debated).
Step 4: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (if available within 8-24 hours).
Step 5: Systemic anticoagulation/thrombolytics (if indicated by neuro-consult).

content.explanation: S: Sudden vision loss, T: Thinning of vessels, O: Ocular massage, K: Kidney function check (for contrast), E: ESR/CRP for GCA.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Cilioretinal artery sparing: Occurs in 15-30% of eyes, preserving central visual acuity.
Always listen for carotid bruits.
Follow-up for NVI/NVA (Neovascularization) at 4-6 weeks.
Prognosis is generally poor; no randomized trial has proven superiority of a single treatment.
